cells.tense: Right now you are standing where nothing is settled and moving anyway.
cells.ask: Make one small decision today that does not need defending — pick it, do it, note how the timing felt in your body. Then let it stand without revisiting it.
cells.core:
You're at a point where nothing has collapsed into one shape yet, and you're not frozen there. You can move while the picture is still open, and your decisions land cleanly because you're not overriding yourself to make them. That's rarer than it sounds.

What's working is that you haven't mistaken possibility for a problem to solve. You're holding many options without needing to kill them off early, and when you do choose, the choice comes from somewhere steady. The way back to this is the same as the way through it: let what you see land before you explain it. Say the thing in one sentence, then stop. No follow-up, no justification.
cells.sheetLine: You can decide while it's still open, and it holds.
cells.verb: move from raw possibility into a decided course without needing permission
cells.place: the open field before anything has been chosen yet

cells.tense: You are bracing for a future outcome that hasn't happened and cannot be written in.
cells.ask: Pick one open question and set a single condition for what would make you act — a date, a signal, a person's answer. Write it down. When that condition hits, you move. Until then, you don't.
cells.core:
You're trying to force the unformed into a shape ahead of time. Every open possibility gets a plan attached to it before it has a chance to show what it is, and the planning has become the relationship. The clarity you want is already in you — you're just spending it on futures that haven't arrived.

What you're actually chasing is the relief of having decided before you're forced to. But possibility doesn't respond to pressure. It collapses on its own time, and you keep pre-collapsing it to feel safe. When you stop reaching ahead for the answer, you'll notice you already handle what's in front of you well. The muscle is there. It's just pointed at the wrong future.
cells.sheetLine: You're deciding futures that haven't asked you yet.
cells.verb: move from raw possibility into a decided course without needing permission

cells.tense: You are standing at a threshold that is already behind you, still waiting for permission.
cells.ask: Name one thing you already moved past but keep re-opening. Tell one person it's done, in plain words. Not that you're working on it — that it's finished. Let their response be whatever it is.
cells.core:
You went through a door a while back and you're still at it. The waiting has its own shape now — you hold a decision private, the way you'd hold something that would break if you said it out loud. So it stays undecided in the telling, even though it isn't undecided in the living.

You still know how to move from open to decided. You do it in small ways all the time without noticing. What stopped is the declaring. Saying it out loud feels like it would put the thing at risk, so you keep it close. The next step isn't more certainty. It's telling one person what you already did, and letting that be enough.
cells.sheetLine: You already crossed the threshold. You're still asking permission.

cells.tense: You are already steering something you talk about as if it were steering itself.
cells.ask: Find one thing you keep calling 'the situation' or 'how it worked out.' Say 'I decided that' about it, out loud, once, to nobody in particular. Then notice what shifts in how it sits with you.
cells.core:
You are already moving things from open to decided. It happens in how you answer questions, what you commit to, what you quietly let go of. The picking is running constantly. You just describe it as circumstance.

It's not the moving that's absent — it's that you haven't claimed it as yours. You give the shape you create to timing, to other people, to how things unfolded. When you don't name your own decisions, you also can't feel their weight or their shape. The move is real. The saying-so hasn't caught up. Naming one thing you decided, even a small one, puts the pen back in your hand where it already is.
cells.sheetLine: The picking is already happening. You keep calling it circumstance.

attempts.check: The unsupported claim: 'Command' as a capacity is not something I can verify the person has, only that the record places this card in this seat, and the imagery of 'unstoppable clarity' risks overstating a felt condition into a fixed trait. A reasonable reader could say 'I don't feel commanding at all,' so the ask must never depend on them agreeing with the reading. The sentence that serves the writer more than the person is any version of 'you already know' that turns a description into a verdict. If my read is wrong, the asks still stand as small, doable acts that teach something about their own timing and permission.
